newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche unit to offer banking on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche unit to offer banking on Internet.

text.p: Bank 24 AG, direct banking unit of Deutsche Bank AG, said on Wednesday it would make its services available via the Internet starting October 15 as part of a bid to become German market leader in branchless banking.
The bank, which operates through an around-the-clock communications center, said computer access would make its services more convenient and less expensive.
Customers will be able to review their accounts, transfer funds, pay bills, and soon buy shares through their personal computers, from home or from anywhere in the world.
"This will allow us to give our customers exactly what they have been looking for," Bank 24 board member Bernd Erlingheuser told a news conference.
Bank 24 aims to break even by 1999 and be the leader in the German direct banking market, added Bank 24 chief executive Thomas Holtrop.
"Our experience shows that German consumers have to get used to friendly service, the way we offer it," Holtrop said.
The bank, which now has 60,000 accounts after 13 months in operation, aims to have 100,000 by the end of this year and 500,000 by the year 2000.
"By offering internet banking we hope to add 60,000 to our customer base by the end of 1997," Erlingheuser said.

Bank officials said about 500,000 to 750,000 Germans now use direct banking services, but that the potential market was about 8.5 million. Four of Germany's top five banks have formed direct banking units.
Holtrop said the market was still too small to give any meaningful estimates of current market share.
Bank 24, which has 350 employees, hopes to lure customers to its internet site at http://www.bank24.de by charging no account fees for those who use computers to access their accounts.
Even now, 16 percent of its customers do so, via online services such as Deutsche Telekom's T-Online. 59 percent of its business comes via telephone, and 25 percent via mail or fax.
The bank offers a full range of services including credit cards, savings, checking and investment accounts and brokerage.
Bank 24 said its average customer profile is the same as the average computer user: well educated, professional between 20 and 49 years old, with a net monthly household income over 4,000 marks.
The average checking account balance at Bank 24 is 4,000 marks, the average savings account 12,500 marks, and the average time deposit 30,000 marks.
"The number of deposits is not the only relevant fact. What counts is the quality of the customer relationship, the volume of the transactions," Holtrop said.
Cross-selling of bank products will be increasingly important in the bank's marketing strategy, he said.
